text.text: Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate the ability of VoxelMap, a deep learning framework for 3D respiratory motion estimation, to generate volumetric images in real-time from 2D projections acquired for two deformable lung phantoms on a clinical interventional C-arm angiography system.
Materials and Methods: VoxelMap was evaluated using the PixelPrint 4D and Casper deformable physical thoracic respiratory phantoms.
Four-dimensional cone-beam CT (4D CBCT) images acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system were used for network training and volumetric ground truth.
Prediction accuracy was evaluated on withheld respiratory phases using structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and peak signalto-noise ratio (PSNR).
Model inference time was measured to assess suitability for continuous real-time processing.
Deep ensembles were also used to assess model uncertainty.
Correlation between ensemble uncertainty and prediction error was evaluated for both phantoms.
Results: VoxelMap achieved high prediction accuracy across withheld respiratory phases in both physical phantoms.
SSIM values exceeded 0.92 in all experiments, with a higher performance observed for the Casper phantom (0.969-0.973) than for the PixelPrint 4D phantom (0.927-0.943).
Model inference times were less than 15 ms for both phantoms which is compatible with real-time processing.
Ensemble uncertainty was positively correlated with prediction error in both phantoms, indicating that higher uncertainty was associated with less accurate volumetric predictions.

Conclusions: Our study demonstrated that VoxelMap generates accurate volumetric deformations of respiratory anatomy from projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm system, with computational inference times compatible with continuous processing.

By deriving volumetric information directly from two-dimensional fluoroscopic projections, VoxelMap has the potential to augment continuous fluoroscopic guidance with continuously updated volumetric information.
Ensemble uncertainty may provide a potentially useful indicator of prediction reliability.
Further studies using clinically representative training data and patient studies is required to establish clinical utility.

text.text: Specifically, CBCT imaging in thoracic intervention supports procedural navigation and confirmation of probe placement, increasing navigational success and diagnostic yield [7, 6, 8, 9].

text.text: However, CBCT and all pre-intervention 3D scans necessarily represent outdated information rather than continuous updates of the current state of anatomy [13].

text.text: Furthermore, dynamic anatomical changes including atelectasis and bronchoscope-induced airway deformation can obscure target lesions on intra-procedural CBCT, reducing the diagnostic yield of CBCTguided bronchoscopy [15, 16].

text.text: Digital tomosynthesis (DTS) attempts to provide depth information with a lower acquisition burden, using a limited angle acquisition with fewer projections to produce a quasi-3D reconstruction [17].

text.text: However, the limited angle acquisition results in poor depth resolution which limits the role of DTS in providing reliable 3D localisation for thoracic interventions [18, 17].

text.text: Neither CBCT nor DTS provide continuously updated volumetric information throughout an intervention.
Currently, there is no continuously updated volumetric guidance derived from 2D fluoroscopic images.
One approach to this problem is VoxelMap, a deep learning framework for real-time volumetric imaging during image guided interventions.
VoxelMap trains a neural network to learn patient-specific correspondences between intra-procedural 2D imaging and the underlying 3D anatomy.

Originally developed in the context of image-guided radiotherapy, this framework enables the generation of continuous real-time volumetric reconstructions by using existing fluoroscopic imaging to deform a reference volumetric image.

VoxelMap has demonstrated the production of volumetric deformations with a high similarity to ground truth on several physical and synthetic phantoms, demonstrating algorithmic feasibility for reconstructing respiratory motion [19, 20].
text.formatted: VoxelMap has demonstrated the production of volumetric deformations with a high similarity to ground truth on several physical and synthetic phantoms, demonstrating algorithmic feasibility for reconstructing respiratory motion <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: The next translational step is demonstrating that VoxelMap achieves accurate volumetric deformations using projections acquired on clinical interventional systems and physical respiratory phantoms.
The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in an interventional setting raises questions regarding the reliability and safety of model predictions.

As deep learning networks are prone to unpredictable failures, transparency and explainability in model development and validation are critical to establish clinician trust and support safe clinical adoption [21, 22].
text.formatted: As deep learning networks are prone to unpredictable failures, transparency and explainability in model development and validation are critical to establish clinician trust and support safe clinical adoption <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians have shared that explainability involves models highlighting where their predictions may be unreliable; models that provide transparency around their limitations may remain acceptable despite underperformance [23].
text.formatted: Clinicians have shared that explainability involves models highlighting where their predictions may be unreliable; models that provide transparency around their limitations may remain acceptable despite underperformance <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Clinician mistrust is a key barrier to the adoption of deep learning in healthcare and uncertainty estimation has been proposed as a mechanism to identify potentially inaccurate predictions and support clinical trust [24].
text.formatted: Clinician mistrust is a key barrier to the adoption of deep learning in healthcare and uncertainty estimation has been proposed as a mechanism to identify potentially inaccurate predictions and support clinical trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: An uncertainty estimate that is correlated with prediction error could indicate when model predictions should be interpreted with greater caution.
Deep ensembles are an established method to estimate the uncertainty 2 of model prediction [25].
text.formatted: Deep ensembles are an established method to estimate the uncertainty 2 of model prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, in this study, we extended the VoxelMap architecture with a deep ensemble network and evaluated the correlation between prediction uncertainty and prediction error.

This approach produces both a volumetric prediction and an estimate of its reliability, addressing two key requirements for the interventional application of VoxelMap: continuous volumetric information and confidence in the resulting predictions.

To address the need for continuously updated and reliable volumetric information in interventional settings, the contributions of this paper are: (1) first demonstration of real-time volumetric imaging using 2D projections acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system; (2) evaluation of VoxelMap prediction performance across two motion programmable physical respiratory phantoms and; (3) leveraging deep ensembles to provide an intuitive indicator of model uncertainty.

VoxelMap is a neural network which takes as input a target 2D projection, a reference 2D projection corresponding to phase 1, and a reference 3D image corresponding to phase 1 and outputs the predicted target 3D image corresponding to the target 2D projection.
The VoxelMap architecture is composed of an encoder-decoder architecture followed by an integration layer and a spatial transformation module [19, 20].

text.text: Individual models for both phantoms were trained using the same VoxelMap architecture and training protocol.
The objective function for training was the mean absolute error (MAE) where for each voxel x, P is the value in the predicted 3D image and G is the value in the ground-truth 3D image.
We extend the VoxelMap architecture with a deep ensemble network.

Following Lakshminarayanan (2016), 4 additional VoxelMap neural networks are instantiated with the same 5 architecture and trained on the same training dataset and only differ by initial weights and data order, to produce a total of 5 models for uncertainty estimation [25].

text.text: The voxel-wise ensemble prediction is defined as the mean of the output of each neural network, and the voxel-wise ensemble uncertainty is defined as the standard deviation of the output of each neural network.
Two deep ensembles were trained on each phantom.
Each ensemble was trained with one phase excluded such that the training dataset for each ensemble consisted of all 2D projections that did not correspond to the excluded phase.
The evaluation dataset consisted of the 397 2D projections corresponding to the excluded phase.

The phases excluded for each phantom were (a) the phase corresponding to end exhalation as end exhalation is relatively anatomically stable and reproducible and (b) the phase corresponding to mid-inhalation to test whether more unstable imaging positions affect accuracy [28].

2D projections in the training and evaluation dataset were linearly HU-normalized to [0, 1] using intensities from all projections in the training dataset.
The 5 neural networks within each ensemble were trained independently with the Adam learning algorithm with the learning rate 1 × 10 -5 and batch size 4 for 100 epochs.
The training dataset was randomly split 90/10 into training and validation sets.
The model parameterisation with the lowest validation loss was saved for evaluation.

Deep learning experiments used the PyTorch framework and were performed on a NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU with 48 GB memory, requiring 6-8 hours for each neural network and 30-40 hours for each ensemble.
Inference time is defined as the time taken for a single forward pass through each model in the ensemble.
The mean and standard deviation of the model inference times was calculated over 392 2D projections corresponding to the excluded phase, excluding n = 5 warm-up projections.

text.text: In this study, VoxelMap demonstrated accurate volumetric representations of respiratory anatomy from 2D projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm system.
VoxelMap maintained high prediction accuracy for withheld respiratory phases across two physical respiratory phantoms while achieving sub-15 ms model inference times.

These findings address key limitations of current interventional image-guidance techniques: fluoroscopy provides continuous procedural imaging but limited 3D anatomical information, whereas volumetric techniques including CBCT and DTS provide 3D information but require dedicated acquisitions and therefore do not provide continuously updated volumetric information throughout an intervention [13, 14, 17].

text.text: By deriving volumetric information from fluoroscopic projections, VoxelMap has the potential to complement existing interventional workflows.
Image-guided navigation is increasingly used in interventional procedures to localize anatomical targets and provide navigational guidance [29, 30].

text.text: However, the spatial relationship between targets, anatomy, and instruments can change during an intervention [15, 14].

text.text: For thoracic procedures, pre-procedural CT can become inaccurate as patient anatomy changes with respiratory motion [31, 32, 33].

text.text: Intra-procedural CBCT addresses some of these limitations by providing intermittent real-time volumetric information, but requires a 200 • rotational acquisition and anatomical accuracy may be reduced by respiratory motion during image acquisition [13, 34, 35].

text.text: Therefore, there is an unmet need for approaches that can provide volumetric information without interrupting the continuous fluoroscopic workflow. 17 Although this study focuses on thoracic interventions, potential applications of our approach extend across image-guided interventions which require 3D localisation of anatomy and instruments using 2D continuously acquired fluoroscopic images.

text.text: Intra-procedural respiratory and other forms of anatomical motion make maintaining correspondence between 2D projections and the underlying 3D anatomy challenging [15, 36].

text.text: Therefore, a method to produce volumetric information directly from continuous fluoroscopic data may reduce this difficulty.

To our knowledge, our study represents the first demonstration of volumetric imaging of respiratory anatomy potentially suitable for continuous real-time volumetric imaging in an interventional setting.
VoxelMap achieved high structural similarity across withheld respiratory phases in both physical phantoms, with SSIM values exceeding 0.92 in all experiments (Table 3).

text.text: In addition, model inference times were less than 15 ms across both phantoms, demonstrating computational latency likely compatible with continuous real-time processing of fluoroscopic images.
Importantly, these results also demonstrate the first validation of VoxelMap using projections acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system.
In addition, our paper represents the first validation of VoxelMap on the Pixelprint 4D phantom and the Casper phantom.
Evaluation across both respiratory phantoms demonstrates that VoxelMap can generalise across distinct physical respiratory phantoms.
VoxelMap achieved high SSIM values across both phantoms, with higher SSIM than the baseline reference in both phantoms.
Prediction performance was higher on Casper than PixelPrint 4D , with SSIM values of 0.969-0.973 compared with 0.927-0.943, respectively.
This difference may reflect differences in respiratory deformation and phantom characteristics rather than an inherent difference in model performance.
Across projection angles, the variation in SSIM for the Casper phase 8 excluded ensemble was less than 0.02, indicating relatively consistent reconstruction performance across acquisition angles.
Overall, the consistently high prediction accuracy across both phantoms demonstrates the reproducibility of our approach across different physical respiratory models.
The potential use of AI to produce predicted volume deformations means that the ability to identify areas where the model may be unreliable is important for clinical adoption [21, 22, 23].

This may reflect the relatively stable anatomy at peak expiration [28].

text.text: The 4D CBCT images used as training data and volumetric ground truth do not represent routine interventional imaging.

However, our primary aim was to evaluate the volumetric information generated by VoxelMap from projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm, while minimizing other changes from the previously published VoxelMap framework, which used 4D CT [19, 20].
text.formatted: However, our primary aim was to evaluate the volumetric information generated by VoxelMap from projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm, while minimizing other changes from the previously published VoxelMap framework, which used 4D CT <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: The use of 4D CBCT therefore enabled the evaluation of projections acquired on a clinical interventional system while providing volumetric ground truth for quantitative assessment of prediction accuracy.
In particular, the availability of volumetric ground truth across two physical thoracic respiratory phantoms provides a rigorous basis for evaluating the prediction of dynamic 3D anatomy.
Further work is required to investigate network training strategies using data that more closely reflect clinically available imaging.
There are several limitations.
First, as a phantom study, we do not capture effects of changes in patient respiratory motion between pre-procedural imaging and interventional procedures.
Further validation of VoxelMap on patient CT images using realistic imaging protocols is required.
Second, two physical phantoms do not capture the variability in anatomy and respiratory motion across patient populations.
Additional evaluation of VoxelMap across diverse respiratory motion patterns and patient datasets is required to establish generalisability.

Third, although we have demonstrated that VoxelMap inference times are consistent with use in a real-time interventional 18 workflow, we did not evaluate the latency of the complete acquisition to visualisation pipeline.
Further validation of VoxelMap in a more complete interventional workflow is warranted.
Fourth, we have not established the clinical usefulness of the model error-uncertainty correlation.
Further validation using patient data and clinically meaningful error thresholds is required to determine whether uncertainty can reliably identify clinically unacceptable reconstructions.

In conclusion, this study demonstrated that VoxelMap can generate accurate volumetric deformations of respiratory anatomy from 2D projections acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system, with sub-15 ms model inference times across two physical respiratory phantoms.

This represents the first application of VoxelMap to projections acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system and the first validation on the physical PixelPrint 4D  and Casper respiratory phantoms.
We also establish the ensemble uncertainty as a potentially useful indicator of prediction reliability.
To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a volumetric imaging technique which has the potential to provide continuously updated volumetric imaging during an intervention.
